nameStory: The name "water flea" comes from the way these tiny crustaceans hop and jerk through the water with quick, flea-like movements. Despite the name, they're not fleas at all - they're actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters! The scientific name "mendotae" honors Lake Mendota in Wisconsin, where this species was first scientifically described.
description: Daphnia mendotae is a microscopic freshwater crustacean that looks like a tiny, translucent bean swimming through the water. These water fleas are incredibly small - usually less than 2 millimeters long - making them invisible to the naked eye in most cases. Their see-through bodies reveal their internal organs, and they have a distinctive large eye spot and branched swimming antennae. They're filter feeders that swim in jerky, hopping motions through lakes and ponds.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Oval, bean-shaped body that's compressed from side to side, appearing nearly transparent with a slight yellowish tint

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Distinctive jerky, hopping movement through the water using large, branched antennae as paddles

idTips.label: Eye spot
idTips.description: Single prominent dark eye spot visible near the front of the head, easily seen even at low magnification

idTips.label: Shell details
idTips.description: Transparent carapace (shell) that covers most of the body, with visible internal organs including heart and digestive tract

idTips.label: Size reference
idTips.description: Extremely small - typically 1-2mm long, about the size of a grain of sand or smaller

habitat: Found in the open waters of clear, nutrient-poor lakes throughout New England, particularly in deeper waters during summer months. They prefer cooler, well-oxygenated water and are often found in glacial lakes and reservoirs. You'll need a microscope or very strong magnifying glass to spot them, as they're part of the zooplankton community.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water warms, reproducing rapidly through parthenogenesis (asexual reproduction). Best time to find them near the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs, but they often move to deeper, cooler waters during hot weather. Most active during cooler morning and evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Sexual reproduction begins as temperatures drop, with females producing special resting eggs. Population numbers start to decline.
seasonality.winter: Most individuals die off, but hardy resting eggs survive frozen in lake sediments until spring thaw triggers hatching.

funFact: Daphnia can reproduce through "virgin birth" - females can clone themselves without mating, producing dozens of identical daughters in just a few days, making them one of nature's most efficient baby-making machines!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other Daphnia species, which all look remarkably similar under basic magnification. The key is habitat - D. mendotae prefers clearer, less nutrient-rich waters compared to the common water flea (D. pulex) which tolerates more polluted conditions.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "fleas," these are actually crustaceans - they're more closely related to lobsters than to any insect. The "Daphnia" genus is named after Daphne from Greek mythology, the nymph who was transformed into a tree, perhaps referencing how these creatures seem to appear and disappear in the water like magic.
compareHints: Daphnia mendotae is distinguished from the more common Daphnia pulex primarily by its habitat preferences and slightly smaller size. While D. pulex thrives in nutrient-rich, sometimes polluted waters, D. mendotae prefers pristine, clear lakes with low nutrient levels. Under high magnification, D. mendotae tends to have a more elongated body shape compared to the rounder D. pulex.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Daphnia mendotae, the Common Water Flea is generally more robust and adaptable to different water conditions.
